name: TurboKV
workload: 200,000 deterministic 20-byte keys / 400-byte values (84MB, above the 64MiB memtable), single caller, sequential/random fill, overwrite, and batched (100/1000 keys per txn) writes, compression and block cache disabled.
claimed_speedup: Sequential fill: 2.99M ops/s (Fast) / 1.77M (Durable) vs redb Eventual 1,397 ops/s; Sequential batch 1000/txn: 3.72M (Fast) vs redb 134,636 ops/s (~27x, derived from page data); fjall also compared and beaten in most rows
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.88.0; RUSTFLAGS target-feature +aes,+sse2 (x86) or +aes,+neon (ARM) for the Bloom-filter path
hardware: Apple M4 (Mac16,1), 32 GiB RAM, macOS 15.3.2, APFS
tradeoffs: redb's single-key rows under Eventual durability pay a macOS F_BARRIERFSYNC per transaction, which the article itself flags as architectural context rather than a strict like-for-like comparison; single-writer, no distributed/replication features; async/Tokio-based API.
caveats: First-party benchmark (project's own repo), though methodology (hardware, rustc version, protocol, raw JSON artifacts) is unusually complete for a first-party bench. redb's disadvantage is partly an artifact of its stronger default durability mode (macOS fsync barrier) rather than a pure algorithmic difference; author notes 'cross-engine settled timings are not compared.'
found_via: Hacker News: search_by_date query 'embedded key value store' -> 'TurboKV: A fast, embedded key-value store in Rust' (HN:46904206 / HN:46762399)

name: mpedb
workload: 50,000-row seeded table; point-insert, point-select, point-update, and 4-thread contended-writes cells; both none-class (no fsync) and commit-class (durable-on-ack, WAL) durability modes; also volume-backed (tmpfs+xfs disk) control-group re-run.
claimed_speedup: point-select (tmpfs, none-class): mpedb 1,975,698 ops/s vs SQLite 320,201 ops/s (~6.2x); point-select (disk, durable WAL commit-class): mpedb 1,942,515 vs SQLite 762,437 (~2.5x, derived from page data); point-insert (tmpfs, none-class): mpedb 230,660 vs SQLite 115,491 ops/s (~2x); volume-backed re-run: point-select 490,310 vs SQLite 79,619 ops/s (~6.2x, derived from page data)
hardware: Apple M3 Pro, 11 cores, 36 GiB RAM, macOS 26.6 (Darwin 25.6.0); also measured on AMD EPYC-Milan, 2 cores, Linux 6.8
license: LicenseRef-mpedb-1.0 (custom source-available license: free except a one-time USD 0.07/device fee for organizations over $5B revenue/valuation)
tradeoffs: Claims class-for-class parity in durability guarantees (WAL vs WAL, none vs none) with an unusually thorough honesty/controls methodology; embedded/single-process like SQLite (fair architectural comparison, unlike the PostgreSQL rows in the same doc); ABI-compatible libsqlite3 shim for drop-in use.
caveats: License is NOT OSI-approved (custom fair-source-style license with an enterprise device fee) even though free for nearly everyone -- usable/studyable but not a plain permissive open-source license. Very early version (0.1.0). Author is unusually rigorous about noise/methodology pitfalls in the same docs, which supports credibility.
found_via: Hacker News: search_by_date query 'faster than SQLite' -> 'Show HN: MPEdb - Drop in replacement for SQLite3 with concurrency support' (HN:49151702)

name: UnisonDB
workload: Redis-compatible SET benchmark via official redis-benchmark tool: 200k mixed SET/GET ops per run, 50 iterations, 10 parallel clients, 10 pipelined requests, 4 threads, 1KB payloads; UnisonDB configured with LMDB as its B-tree backend.
claimed_speedup: (derived from page data, read off scatter plot) SET throughput ~100,000-135,000 req/s for UnisonDB at ~0.2-0.4ms p50 latency vs ~35,000-42,000 req/s for LMDB at ~0.7-0.85ms p50 latency -- roughly 3x higher throughput and ~3x lower latency
hardware: Apple M2 Pro, 10 cores (6P+4E), 16 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Numbers only shown as a scatter-plot PNG (docs/ubbl_compare.png), no numeric table, so exact figures are read off axes rather than quoted; Go compiler version not stated; UnisonDB's actual local storage is LMDB itself (it wraps LMDB and adds WAL-based streaming/replication), so the throughput delta likely reflects the Redis-protocol server layer/pipelining differences rather than a faster underlying B-tree.
caveats: First-party benchmark, own repo; no compiler/flags stated; results presented only as an image, numbers approximate; UnisonDB literally uses LMDB as its storage engine, so this measures the wrapping server (WALFS/replication layer), not a faster core than LMDB itself -- record with low confidence.
found_via: Hacker News: search 'faster than BoltDB' / 'durable KV store' -> 'Show HN: UnisonDB – Log-native KV database that replicates like a message bus' (HN:45784331 / HN:45871223)

name: BTreePlus
workload: Bulk insert benchmarks of 4M and 1B rows with 32KB pages on NVMe under .NET 9.0/Linux; separate 1-billion-record (14-byte payload) bulk insert vs PostgreSQL with WAL enabled on both.
claimed_speedup: 4M rows: 4.53s (SQLite) vs 1.03s (BTreePlus Pro) = 4.4x; 1B rows: 2410s (SQLite) vs 346s (BTreePlus Pro) = 7x; also ~16% faster than PostgreSQL on a 1B-row WAL-enabled insert (6m08s vs 5m10s)
hardware: NVMe SSD (SQLite comparison, exact CPU not stated); Intel i9-13900 + Samsung 990 PRO NVMe (PostgreSQL comparison)
tradeoffs: The 4.4x/7x-faster numbers are for the closed-source commercial 'Pro Edition' (adds page caching, sharding, range scans); the MIT-licensed 'Community Edition' on GitHub explicitly disables the page cache and is documented as 'not optimized for speed' -- so the actual open-source code does not deliver the claimed speedup.
caveats: Mixed licensing: fast numbers require a paid, closed-source component layered on top of the free MIT core, so the performance claim cannot be independently reproduced from the open-source repo alone. CPU model for the headline SQLite benchmark is not stated (only 'NVMe'); only 9 GitHub stars.
found_via: Hacker News: search 'B-tree database faster than SQLite' -> 'Show HN: BTreePlus – A cache-optimized B+Tree engine for .NET faster than SQLite' (HN:46045384)
